eye.because: House A's ground floor is the clearest sequence. W has the original two ground-floor sash windows. Y has them replaced by a blank shopfront with fascia and sign bracket. Z and X add a railing at A's left side. House B's upper windows are narrow, two-pane sashes with heavy trim in W, and have been widened to wide three-pane openings in Y, Z and X. So W is earliest and Y second. D's gable windows are glazed in W and Y and boarded or shuttered in Z and X (neglect, later). Z and X look the same apart from sub-pixel shifts of the chimney tops. I put Z before X because the chimney tops move down steadily in W, Y, Z, X order (a settling drift), and the same drift fits the other views. That last step is weak. Years are my estimates from style (original sash windows, then a shopfront and large-pane windows, then a balcony railing), not from any date mark. I also compared frames pixel by pixel to find the changes.

street.because: The two pairs are clear. In Y and Z, C's side and gable windows are boarded and D's gable window is glazed. In W and X, C's windows are glazed and D's window is boarded with a Z-braced shutter. The other views show the shopfront and the widened windows arriving between the first and second frames, so the Y/Z pair comes first and the W/X pair last. The order within each pair is a guess. Almost nothing visible separates Y from Z, or W from X, apart from tiny shifts of the chimney tops, clapboard lines and glazing bars. I matched those shifts to the eye view, where the order is known, and they fit a steady downward settling (Z, Y, X, W). Years are estimates.

12m.because: The pairs are clear. In X and W, C's three side and gable windows are shuttered and D's three windows are glazed, which is the early state. In Y and Z, C's windows are glazed and D's three windows are boarded, which is the later state. The order within each pair is only a guess. W and X differ only in chimney-top and clapboard shifts on C and D, and so do Y and Z. I matched those shifts to the street and eye views and they fit one steady settling drift, giving X, W, Y, Z. Years are estimates.

city.because: At A, X has the original ground-floor windows and no shopfront. Z has the blank shopfront but no railing at the left bay. Y and W have the shopfront plus a balcony railing at the left. B's upper windows are narrow in X and wide in Z, Y and W. C is shuttered and D glazed in X and Z; C is glazed and D shuttered in Y and W. That puts X and Z first and second, and Y and W last. House E has an extra ground-floor opening beside its door in X, Z and Y but not in W. The simplest reading is that the opening was removed once, at the end, so W is last. That is the only cue separating Y from W, and it is weak, since the opening could also have been removed and then restored. Years are estimates.
